publicize.e: English public Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English publicize From public + -ize.

d.g: To issue (something, such as printed work) for distribution and/or sale.
d.x: The Times published the investigative piece about the governor both in print and online.

d.g: To announce to the public.
d.x: The Secretary of Health and Human Services published a press release on May 22, 2013.

d.g: To issue the work of (an author).
d.x: Grove Press published many avant-garde authors.

d.g: To disseminate (a message) publicly via a newsgroup, forum, blog, etc.

publish.e: From Middle English publicen (by analogy with banish, finish), from Old French publier, from Latin publicare (“to make public, show or tell to the people, make known, declare, also (and earlier) confiscate for public use”), from publicus (“pertaining to the people, public”); see public.

d.g: A plaintive melancholy whine.
To whimper or whine.
d.x: Although the elderly man felt mounting pain from his illness, he never complained or puled.

d.g: To pipe or chirp.
To fall in a continuous, light dribble.
d.x: ... looked at the puling sky, face upturned to a mirr of rain.

pule.e: From French piauler, a variant of French piailler (“to chirp, cheep”). Compare Italian pigolare (“to cheep as a chicken”).

d.g: To multiply rapidly.
To germinate.
To teem with; to be filled (with).
d.x: I must say the whole of Oxford has become most peculiar suddenly. Last night it was pullulating with women.

pullulate.e: Borrowed from Latin pullulātus, perfect passive participle of pullulō (“sprout forth”), from pullulus (“a young animal, a sprout”), diminutive of pullus.

d.g: To expand and contract rhythmically; to throb or to beat, exhibit a pulse.
To quiver, vibrate, or flash; as to the beat of music.
d.x: The party pulsated with revellers.

d.g: To pulse, to be full of life, energy: to bustle, thrive, flourish.
To produce a recurring increase and decrease of some quantity.

pulsate.e: Perhaps formed within English as a back-formation from pulsation (attested from the early 15th century, in Middle English). …

d.g: To render into dust or powder.
To completely destroy, especially by crushing to fragments or a powder.
To defeat soundly, thrash.
To become reduced to powder; to fall to dust.
d.x: the stone pulverises easily

pulverise.e: From Middle English pulverizen, from Latin pulverizō, pulverizāre, from pulvis (“powder”). Compare French pulvériser. By surface analysis, pulver (“powder”) + -ise.

d.g: American and Oxford British spelling of pulverise.
To hit or strike heavily and repeatedly.
d.x: Rain pummeled the roof.

d.g: To scornfully criticize someone or something.
d.x: The politician was pummeled by the media for his controversial statements.

d.g: Alternative form of pommel.
To add punctuation to.
d.x: That occurrence of "its" needs to be punctuated as "it's".

d.g: To add or to interrupt at regular intervals.
d.x: My father punctuated his tirade with thumps on the desk.

d.g: To emphasize; to stress.
Point-like; consisting of or marked with one or more points.
d.x: Positive HPV 16 hybridization signal in two cervical carcinomas. A punctuate signal (a) and a punctuate and diffuse signal (b).

punctuate.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuātus, perfect passive participle of pūnctuō (“to mark with points”), from Medieval Latin pūnctus (“a point, dot”), from pungō (“to prick, punch”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of punch.

d.g: To cause (a child, student, or someone else being looked after, or a suspect or criminal) to suffer for crime or misconduct, to administer disciplinary action, typically by an authority or a person in authority (for example: a parent, teacher, or police officer).
d.x: If a prince violates the law, then he must be punished like an ordinary person.

d.g: To treat harshly and unfairly.
d.x: Homer, moreover, gives the impression that the Sun punished Odysseus's men; but we are later told that the Sun cannot punish individual men […]

d.g: To handle or beat severely; to maul.
To consume a large quantity of.
d.x: A few moments later, we were all sitting around the veranda of the hunters' dining hall, punishing the gin, as usual.

punish.e: From Middle English punischen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French puniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of punir, from Latin puniō (“to inflict punishment upon”), from poena (“punishment, penalty”); see pain. Displaced Old English wītnian and (mostly, in this sense) wrecan.

d.g: To become a pupa.
d.x: But first. Attend me, as I pupate!

pupate.e: English pupa Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos Proto-Italic *-ātos Latin -ātuslbor. English -ate English pupate From pupa + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To cleanse, or rid of impurities.
d.x: The modern arts deviate from the standards set forth by the divine—art should be used to purify one’s heart and improve one’s morality.

d.g: To free from guilt or sin.
To become pure.

purify.e: From Middle English purifien, purifyen, from Old French purifier, purifiier, from Latin pūrificō, pūrificāre, from pūrus (“pure; clean”).

d.g: To take the property of another, often in breach of trust; to appropriate wrongfully; to steal.
d.x: Had from his wakeful custody purloined / The guarded gold.

d.g: To commit theft; to thieve.
d.x: The Apostle expressly forbiddeth servants to purloin (Titus 2:10).

purloin.e: From Middle English purloynen (“to remove”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman purloigner (“to put far away”), one of the variants of Old French porloignier. Doublet of prolong.

d.g: Of a purple colour.
A salt of purpuric acid.

purpurate.e: From Latin purpura (“the color purple”) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

d.g: To follow urgently, originally with intent to capture or harm; to chase.
d.x: pursue one's dreams

d.g: To follow, travel down (a particular way, course of action etc.).
d.x: Her rival pursued a quite different course.

d.g: To aim for, go after (a specified objective, situation etc.).
d.x: He even stands to gain in world terms: his noisy critics strengthen his projected image of a man determined to pursue peace with Palestinians.

d.g: To participate in (an activity, business etc.); to practise, follow (a profession).

pursue.e: From Middle English pursuen, from Anglo-Norman pursure, poursuire etc., from Latin prōsequor (though influenced by persequor). Doublet of prosecute.

d.g: To furnish or provide.
d.x: Giue no ods to your foes, but do puruay / Your selfe of sword before that bloudy day:

d.g: To procure; to get.
d.x: I mean to purvey me a wife after the fashion of the children of Benjamin.

purvey.e: From Middle English purveyen, from Anglo-Norman purveer, purveir et al., Old French porveeir, porveoir, from Latin prōvidēre (“to provide”). Doublet of provide; compare prudent.

d.g: To move silently, stealthily, or furtively.
To act timidly or cautiously.
d.x: The TSSA union said the Government should "stop pussyfooting around" and place Euston at the heart of the transformative rail project.

d.g: To use euphemistic language or circumlocution.
d.x: "Then you talk up! And plain! What's there to be so pussyfooting about?"

d.g: A teetotaller.
d.x: "We keep off that road like a pussyfoot keeps off whiskey. Get it out of your bean that we're exploring a deserted ruin."

pussyfoot.e: From pussy (“feline”) + foot; because of the light and careful tread of cats.

d.g: To fester or rot and exude a fetid stench.
To become filled with a pus-like or bile-like substance.
To reach an advanced stage of decomposition.
To become gangrenous.
